Lab 131204 — First-Pass USV Analysis

Dataset summary
  • 17 couples (12 cross-strain + 5 same-strain), recorded 2013-12-04
  • ~14 hours of audio split into 25,770 × 2-second WAV chunks at 300 kHz
  • 41,061 USV calls detected by the production CNN (post-300 ms duration filter)
  • 40,787 calls kept after pairing with DeepSqueak acoustic features
Report generated 2026-05-15 · Pipeline: detection → DeepSqueak features → 3 classifiers + repertoire stats

At a glance

Five findings emerged from this first-pass analysis. Two are new, two confirmed earlier signals from the post-labeling handoff, and one is descriptive (repertoire composition).

#FindingStatusHeadline
1Scattoni-7 syllable distribution descriptive Flat & Chevron together make up over half of all calls
2Continuous repertoire structure new Density-based clustering finds one dominant continuous mode; unimodality survives the size-control down-sample test
3Tier signal confirmed Manual-review tier carries 2.4× more Short and 2.3× more Complex calls (effect size V = 0.25, medium-large)
4Couple-keep-set signal confirmed Four noise-prone couples have distinct repertoires (V = 0.17, small-medium)
5Two independent noise mechanisms new A duration noise (filtered out) and a residual 49 kHz tonal noise (survived all filters) hit different couples

Finding 1 — Syllable distribution descriptive

Using the standard Scattoni-2008 7-type taxonomy (a rule-based classifier applied to each call's acoustic features):

Syllable typeCount%
Flat 12,13429.75
Chevron 9,132 22.39
Down 5,884 14.43
Short 5,364 13.15
Complex 3,651 8.95
Up 3,545 8.69
Frequency Jump 1,077 2.64

Flat calls (steady tone, little frequency modulation) and Chevron calls (rise-then-fall) dominate. Frequency Jump calls — sharp discontinuous shifts mid-call — are rare (2.6%).

Finding 2 — Continuous repertoire structure new

The Scattoni labels above assume seven distinct categories. To test whether the data actually cluster into distinct types, we ran two independent clustering methods on the raw acoustic features:

  • DeepSqueak k-means (k=26) — forces the data into 26 partitions by design
  • UMAP + HDBSCAN — density-based; lets the data decide how many clusters exist

HDBSCAN groups events that genuinely cluster in feature space. On the full lab dataset, it returns one dominant cluster containing 71% of all calls, one small outlier cluster (~8%), one tiny residual-noise cluster (244 calls — see Finding 5), and 20% noise points. By comparison, the wild-mouse dataset (3452) produces 5+ separable clusters with the same algorithm settings.

Size-control check (down-sample test). A natural objection is that the lab has 40,787 calls while wild 3452 has only 7,921 — could the unimodality just reflect more data smoothing out clusters? We stratified-sampled the lab to n=7,920 (matching 3452) preserving couple proportions, and re-ran HDBSCAN with identical settings. Result: 2 clusters with 0.2% noise; the mega-cluster grew to 91%. Unimodality is not a dataset-size artifact.

Interpretation. Lab USVs appear to occupy a continuous acoustic space rather than discrete categories. The Scattoni labels remain useful as bookkeeping coordinates, but they should not be read as evidence for distinct call-types in this cohort.

Finding 3 — Tier signal confirmed

Each detected call carries a tier from the upstream labeling pipeline: auto_accept (high confidence, n=29,790) or manual_review (lower confidence, n=10,997). The post-labeling handoff predicted these two tiers would have different syllable mixes — a residual quality artifact rather than a biological difference.

TestNχ²pCramér's V
tier (auto_accept vs manual_review) 40,7872,551.3≈ 00.250

Effect size V = 0.25 sits between "medium" (0.3) and "small" (0.1) — meaningful, not subtle. Manual-review carries 2.4× more Short and 2.3× more Complex calls than auto_accept.

Implication for Phase 3. Primary wild-vs-lab statistics should be computed on auto_accept-tier calls only, to avoid contaminating biological comparisons with detection-quality artifacts.

Finding 5 — Two independent noise mechanisms new

While inspecting the small HDBSCAN clusters, we found that one of them (244 events) has a very specific acoustic signature that does not look like a real USV:

FeatureCluster 1 medianReal USV typical range
Peak frequency49 kHz60–80 kHz
Bandwidth 9.8 kHz 30–60 kHz
Sinuosity 1.04 1.5–2.0 (FM curvature)
Tier 89.8% auto_accept—

That profile — low-frequency, narrow-band, no curvature, but high-confidence — describes a sustained tonal artifact the CNN was confident-wrong about.

The mechanism is independent from the duration-noise cohort. The four duration-noise-prone couples (Finding 4) were m1fm1, m1fm2, m1fm4, m3fm3. The residual tonal-noise events concentrate in a different set: m5fm5 (54), m4fm4 (47), m3fm1 (33), m4fm2 (31) — these four couples account for 68% of the residual-noise cluster.

So at least two distinct noise mechanisms are operating in this dataset:

MechanismEventsCouples concentrated inWhere it ends up
A — Duration noise~502 (already filtered) m1fm1, m1fm2, m1fm4, m3fm3 Removed by <300 ms filter
B — Residual tonal artifact244 m5fm5, m4fm4, m3fm1, m4fm2 Survived all current filters; 89.8% in auto_accept tier

For Phase 3: a second couple-aware noise guard targeting Mechanism B's cohort may be worth adding before computing wild-vs-lab repertoire statistics.

Looking ahead — wild-mouse comparison context

Phase 3 will compare this lab cohort against the wild-mouse dyads we have on hand. Four wild-mouse dyads are now available, and their total event counts span two orders of magnitude — the range is much wider than you might guess:

Wild dyadWAVsUSV eventsNotes
5970 (lmt_034) 6,4007,575 High-USV reference cohort
9252 11,580597 Normally quieter cohort
3452 (lmt_035, reviewed subset) 853401 Normally quieter cohort
2379 (lmt_031) 1,28031 Very short cohort — only 31 high-confidence events from 1,280 WAVs (1.64% file yield, 48× lower per-file rate than 5970). Will appear in Phase 3 only as a descriptive minority cohort, not a primary statistical comparator.
Implication for Phase 3 wild-vs-lab statistics. Raw event counts cannot be compared directly — they confound vocal output with recording duration and cohort size. Primary statistics will be normalized by per-file rate or recording duration. The 2379 cohort is small enough (n = 31) that the usual repertoire-clustering tools (DeepSqueak k = 26 k-means, UMAP + HDBSCAN with default min_cluster_size) are data-starved; only descriptive per-call statistics will be reported for it.

Open questions for Mickey

  1. Should we proceed to Phase 3 (wild-vs-lab statistical comparison)?
  2. Is the continuous (unimodal) repertoire structure biologically expected for inbred lab strains? It is the most novel finding and the down-sample test rules out a size artifact, but it would be useful to know whether this matches prior expectations or is genuinely surprising.
  3. The four residual-noise couples (m5fm5, m4fm4, m3fm1, m4fm2) — do they share an environmental factor (same room, same cage rack, same recording session timing) that could produce a sustained 49 kHz tonal artifact?
  4. Lab recording protocol — critical for any rate (calls/min) comparison. The manifest shows 83 recordings, each ~600 s (10 min), at three fixed timepoints (10:00, 14:00, 18:00) on 9 days. To make a fair lab-vs-wild rate comparison we need to know:
    • What was the total recording duration per dyad? Was it exactly the ~10-min × N timepoints captured in the manifest, or were longer recordings made and only these slices preserved? Was anything recorded outside the 10/14/18 windows?
    • Why exactly 10 minutes? Fixed duration suggests a deliberate protocol (e.g., novel-partner introduction + standardized recording window). What was the behavioral context? Was the male introduced to the female just before each recording, or were they continuously housed?
    • Light cycle and circadian alignment. Were recordings at 10/14/18 during the mice's subjective day (sleep) or subjective night (active)? Did the room use a reversed LD cycle (common in vivariums)? This determines whether the lab "denominator" represents an active or inactive behavioral state.
    • Pair-housing context. Were dyads continuously co-housed and recorded periodically, or only paired during the recording window? (This affects whether the rate measures vocal availability over the full dyad lifespan, or just during introduction stress / courtship arousal.)
    Why this matters: Wild recordings are LMT activity-triggered (2.147-s clips fired only when sound energy is detected; ~3% duty cycle on a 24-29 hour housing window for cohort 2379). Lab recordings are scheduled fixed-duration ~10-min clips that include silence. The denominators of "calls per minute" are therefore measuring fundamentally different things, and the apparent 5× lab>wild raw rate cannot be claimed as a strain effect without the missing protocol context. Until this is resolved we will report within-bout metrics (intra-bout ICI, calls/bout, bout duration) — which don't depend on what wasn't recorded — as the primary cross-strain comparison.
  5. Behavioral metadata to pair with each lab recording. Were any behavioral observations logged simultaneously (e.g., mounting, sniffing, chasing, latency to first call)? Even rough per-recording notes ("active", "quiet", "first 2 min were introduction") would let us interpret the calls-per-bout distribution.
  6. Video of the mice courting. To ground the call sequences in observed behavior, we need video footage of a dyad recording session — ideally time-synchronized to one of the 10:00 / 14:00 / 18:00 audio recordings so the two streams can be aligned frame-accurately. Even a single ~10-min clip would let us:
    • Confirm that the recordings actually capture courtship (mounting, chasing, anogenital sniffing) rather than a different behavioral state (introduction stress, defensive posturing, undisturbed rest).
    • Anchor specific call bursts to discrete behaviors — e.g., does a burst of Complex calls coincide with mounting attempts, or with the female's rejection response?
    • Substitute for the per-recording behavioral notes asked for in (5): if video exists, we can score it ourselves and don't need to rely on retrospective annotations.
    Why this matters: Without behavioral ground-truth the 5× lab>wild call-rate signal and the within-bout structure findings are uninterpretable as “courtship” per se — they could equally reflect introduction stress or any other male–female interaction. One synchronized video would unblock the behavioral interpretation of every cross-cohort finding in this report.

Methodology — short version

  • Source: 25,770 × 2-second WAV chunks at 300 kHz from 17 couples recorded 2013-12-04, ~14 h total.
  • Detection: production CNN with soft-notch preprocessing (artifact suppression in the carrier-frequency band).
  • Cleaning: <300 ms duration filter (post-labeling handoff finding); 41,061 calls kept of the original detections.
  • Features: DeepSqueak Excel export — 16 standardized acoustic measures per call, including call length, peak/low/high frequency, bandwidth, slope, sinuosity, tonality, mean power.
  • Classifiers run:
    • Scattoni-2008 rule-based 7-type taxonomy
    • DeepSqueak k-means (k=26, hard-coded)
    • UMAP + HDBSCAN (data-driven; default min_cluster_size=50, min_samples=10)
  • Repertoire comparison: per-cohort Scattoni-7 proportions with chi-square tests and Cramér's V effect sizes.
  • Down-sample test: stratified sample of the lab cohort to n=7,920 (matching wild 3452), preserving per-couple proportions (random_state=42), then re-ran UMAP+HDBSCAN with default settings.
